features.name: Bangalore North Taluk study extent
features.location_description: Bangalore North Taluk, Bangalore Urban district, Karnataka; 799 sq km

narrative.analysis: Bangalore North taluk covers 799 square kilometres, about the size of a large city district, and is home to roughly 3.5 lakh people (2011 census) in 199 villages grouped under 39 village councils and 6 hoblies. It gets a modest 870 mm of normal yearly rain. Its corners stretch roughly from longitude 77.37 to 77.74 east and latitude 12.91 to 13.23 north (the report prints the lat/long labels swapped; the numbers are corrected here). It borders Bangalore South, Bangalore East and Bangalore Rural.

A monitoring well (PZ means it is watched for water levels rather than pumped for supply) drilled about 200 metres down into granite-like rock near the Geological Survey office. It met water-bearing cracks between roughly 11 and 32 metres depth and yields about half a litre per second, a slow domestic-scale trickle, like filling a bucket in about half a minute.

The star well of the whole study: a test well at the Indian Institute of Science campus, drilled about 163 metres into granite-like rock with veins. It struck water-bearing cracks at four depth bands, including a deep one near the bottom (158-163 m), and the resting water level sits about 55 metres below ground. It yields 4.26 litres per second, the highest of all 14 test wells, enough to fill a bucket in a few seconds. It shows that deep cracks in this rock can occasionally pay off well.

A test well in Cubbon Park, drilled about 116 metres into granite-like rock. Its water-bearing cracks are shallow (roughly 9-34 m), and water stands just 2 metres below the surface, so this spot taps the shallow weathered zone almost at ground level. It yields about 1 litre per second, a modest but usable supply.

features.name: BWSSB Yelahanka, Jakkur (EW)
features.location_description: BWSSB Yelahanka, Jakkur, Bangalore North Taluk

narrative.analysis: A test well near Yelahanka and Jakkur, drilled about 139 metres through broken and weathered granite-like rock. It met cracks at three depths (around 59, 90 and 138 m), water stands very shallow at just 1.6 metres below ground, and it yields 0.75 litres per second. The shallow resting water level means the shallow aquifer here is full near the surface.

A cautionary well at Rachnehalli: drilled about 101 metres into weathered granite-like rock but met no water-bearing cracks at all. It yields a negligible 0.08 litres per second, barely a drip. It is the clearest proof in this report that depth alone does not make water in hard rock; without cracks, there is almost nothing to pump.

features.name: IIM, Bannerghatta Road (EW)
features.location_description: IIM, Bannerghatta Road, Bangalore North Taluk — printed coordinate retained as-reported but quarantined (implausible for Bannerghatta Road)

narrative.analysis: A test well listed for the IIM Bannerghatta Road area, drilled about 109 metres with one crack zone around 51-55 m. Water rests about 31 metres down and it yields a small 0.22 litres per second. Note its printed map coordinate (latitude 13.89555) does not fit Bannerghatta Road and looks like a typo, so the record is kept in the table but left off the map.

The deepest hole in the study: a 310-metre monitoring well at Hessarghatta into granite, far deeper than any other well. It met only one thin crack band around 172 m, water stands extremely deep at about 161 metres below ground, and the report records no usable yield. Going deeper did not help here; below the cracked zone the rock is solid and dry.

A test well at Vidyanagar that reached about 209 metres through granite-like rock, meeting cracks at seven different depths from 32 m down to the bottom. The report records no pumping result for it, so unlike its neighbours we cannot say how much water it would actually give; it is evidence of cracked rock at many levels, not of a proven supply.

A test well at Yelahanka that goes 200 metres down through granite-like rock, striking cracks at about 31, 49, 64 and 140 metres. With 1.4 litres per second it is among the stronger producers in the study (behind the IISc well at 4.26 and two Hessarghatta wells at 1.75), showing that several stacked crack bands can add up to a useful supply.

The second-deepest hole in the study (about 241 m) at Hessarghatta, cut through granite-like rock mixed with quartz. Its cracks are all in the upper half (roughly 13-89 m), yet it yields 1.75 litres per second, among the best in the area. The water comes from the shallow-to-mid cracks, not from the extra depth below them.

features.name: Hassarghatta OW II (OW)
features.location_description: Hassarghatta OW II, Bangalore North Taluk

narrative.analysis: A 100-metre observation well at Hessarghatta (one of a monitored pair) bored through granite-like rock with quartzite. It met four crack bands between 15 and 68 metres and yields 1.75 litres per second, matching the deeper Hessarghatta well beside it, which suggests the productive cracks here sit in the upper 100 metres.

features.name: Hassarghatta OW II (OW)
features.location_description: Hassarghatta OW II, Bangalore North Taluk

narrative.analysis: The shallowest test hole in the study at just over 50 metres, the companion Hessarghatta observation well. Its cracks are all shallow (15-46 m) and it yields only 0.13 litres per second, a thin trickle. Beside its 100-metre neighbour giving 1.75 litres per second, it shows how much yield can vary between two holes in the same ground.

A monitoring well at NIMHANS drilled 100 metres into granite-like rock with light-coloured pegmatite veins. It met two crack bands (roughly 47-51 m and 69-72 m), water stands about 5 metres below ground, and it yields about 1 litre per second: a typical mid-range result for this taluk's fractured rock.

chart_series.title: Annual rainfall, Bangalore North 2006–2019
chart_series.description: Normal 870 mm over 56 rainy days (9 gauges); driest 2013 (583 mm), wettest 2017 (1678 mm).

chart_series.title: Stage of groundwater development 2009–2020

chart_series.title: Net irrigated area by source
chart_series.description: Only tube/borewells irrigate (5125 units, 2251 ha); 205 tanks irrigate nothing.

chart_series.title: GWRA-2020 availability vs draft
chart_series.description: Gross draft 2931.98 ham against 2023.34 ham availability: stage 144.91%, Over Exploited.

chart_series.title: Nitrate range vs drinking limit
chart_series.description: Nitrate exceeds the 45 mg/l BIS limit in parts of both aquifers.

chart_series.title: Fluoride range vs drinking limit
chart_series.description: Fluoride is essentially within the 1.5 mg/l limit; the printed Aquifer-I maximum (1.56) marginally exceeds it while the report text and Fig 11 indicate <=1.5, so treat the shallow aquifer as near-limit (Q-07).

chart_series.title: Path from 2023 ham to 2718 ham (AR + drip savings)
Stage of development: today vs after measures
chart_series.description: Still above 100% after all measures, but the gap shrinks from ~45 to ~8 points.

chart_series.title: Exploration wells: drilled depth vs discharge (depth alone does not make water)
chart_series.description: One point per Table 6 well with both drilled depth and numeric discharge printed (11 of 14; blanks and 'negligible' stay missing, never zero). Deepest hole (310 m Hessarghatta PZ) has negligible discharge and is therefore absent here; highest yield is IISc 4.26 lps at 162.5 m. Synthesis view of source rows, linked to well features.

chart_series.title: Exploration-well discharge ranking (Table 6)
chart_series.description: Numeric discharges only, sorted high to low. Wells with blank/negligible discharge in the source are omitted, not zeroed.

chart_series.title: Aquifer-II depth-to-water range, pre vs post monsoon 2019
chart_series.description: Fractured Aquifer-II water levels span a far wider and deeper range than shallow Aquifer-I; monsoon narrows the deep end from 57.38 to 37.50 m bgl.

chart_series.title: Proposed recharge sites by gram panchayat (derived count, 343 sites)
chart_series.description: Deterministic count of Annexure-I/II rows per gram panchayat (20 panchayats for check dams, 17 for percolation tanks). Derived presentation: source rows unchanged; Bangalore (North) panchayat holds the most proposals (64 check dams + 12 tanks). Use as a panchayat filter/companion to the map, not as a surveyed priority ranking.

chart_series.title: Proposed recharge structures by type (344 structures)
chart_series.description: Supply-side package composition from Table 8.1. The single subsurface dyke has no annexure coordinate and stays map-free.

chart_series.title: Monsoon runoff to expected recharge (10% efficiency)
chart_series.description: Of 55.00 MCM available runoff over the 553 sq km feasible area, the plan expects 5.50 MCM (550 ham) recharge at 10% efficiency, for Rs 39.53 Cr. Like-for-like MCM only; cost and area stay in the resource table.

limitations: 293 check-dam and 50 percolation-tank points are tentative representative locations; field/DPR verification required (LM-02/LM-13).
IIM Bannerghatta Road well coordinate retained as-reported in the table but excluded from map geometry (SUB-09).
Fig 10 dark-class label misprints '>750'; treated as 751–2250 per prose, flagged uncertain (Q-09).
Fig 6/7 zone boundaries and Fig 9a/9b thicknesses are figure-derived and approximate (SUB-07/SUB-10).
2020 assessment uses a revised methodology, so its lower base is not directly comparable with 2009–2017 values (Q-06).
3951 ham of treated sewage is piped to Kolar/Chikballapur and unavailable to this taluk (LM-06).
Even after all measures the stage stays at ~108%: still over-exploited, only less so (LM-07).
Panchayat counts (cs-proposals-by-panchayat) and coverage envelopes are deterministic derivations from source coordinates/rows, labelled derived; they are not surveyed priorities or boundaries.
Fluoride source inconsistency: printed Aquifer-I maximum 1.56 mg/l marginally exceeds the 1.5 mg/l limit while report text/Fig 11 indicate <=1.5; shown as near-limit, not comfortably clear (Q-07).

Source facts vs derived synthesis distinguished via status/geometry_origin/confidence.

target_insights.analysis: This is the official Central Ground Water Board aquifer map and management plan for Bangalore North taluk, prepared under the National Aquifer Mapping project for 2020-21. Think of it as a health checkup plus a treatment plan for the underground water beneath this part of Bangalore: it maps the rocks that hold water, measures how much is pumped versus refilled, flags pollution, and proposes small rain-catching structures and water-saving steps. Everything in this viewer comes from that one report.

A monitoring well (PZ means it is watched for water levels rather than pumped for supply) drilled about 200 metres down into granite-like rock near the Geological Survey office. It met water-bearing cracks between roughly 11 and 32 metres depth and yields about half a litre per second, a slow domestic-scale trickle, like filling a bucket in about half a minute.

The star well of the whole study: a test well at the Indian Institute of Science campus, drilled about 163 metres into granite-like rock with veins. It struck water-bearing cracks at four depth bands, including a deep one near the bottom (158-163 m), and the resting water level sits about 55 metres below ground. It yields 4.26 litres per second, the highest of all 14 test wells, enough to fill a bucket in a few seconds. It shows that deep cracks in this rock can occasionally pay off well.

A test well in Cubbon Park, drilled about 116 metres into granite-like rock. Its water-bearing cracks are shallow (roughly 9-34 m), and water stands just 2 metres below the surface, so this spot taps the shallow weathered zone almost at ground level. It yields about 1 litre per second, a modest but usable supply.

A test well near Yelahanka and Jakkur, drilled about 139 metres through broken and weathered granite-like rock. It met cracks at three depths (around 59, 90 and 138 m), water stands very shallow at just 1.6 metres below ground, and it yields 0.75 litres per second. The shallow resting water level means the shallow aquifer here is full near the surface.

A cautionary well at Rachnehalli: drilled about 101 metres into weathered granite-like rock but met no water-bearing cracks at all. It yields a negligible 0.08 litres per second, barely a drip. It is the clearest proof in this report that depth alone does not make water in hard rock; without cracks, there is almost nothing to pump.

A test well listed for the IIM Bannerghatta Road area, drilled about 109 metres with one crack zone around 51-55 m. Water rests about 31 metres down and it yields a small 0.22 litres per second. Note its printed map coordinate (latitude 13.89555) does not fit Bannerghatta Road and looks like a typo, so the record is kept in the table but left off the map.

The deepest hole in the study: a 310-metre monitoring well at Hessarghatta into granite, far deeper than any other well. It met only one thin crack band around 172 m, water stands extremely deep at about 161 metres below ground, and the report records no usable yield. Going deeper did not help here; below the cracked zone the rock is solid and dry.

A test well at Vidyanagar that reached about 209 metres through granite-like rock, meeting cracks at seven different depths from 32 m down to the bottom. The report records no pumping result for it, so unlike its neighbours we cannot say how much water it would actually give; it is evidence of cracked rock at many levels, not of a proven supply.

A test well at Yelahanka that goes 200 metres down through granite-like rock, striking cracks at about 31, 49, 64 and 140 metres. With 1.4 litres per second it is among the stronger producers in the study (behind the IISc well at 4.26 and two Hessarghatta wells at 1.75), showing that several stacked crack bands can add up to a useful supply.

The second-deepest hole in the study (about 241 m) at Hessarghatta, cut through granite-like rock mixed with quartz. Its cracks are all in the upper half (roughly 13-89 m), yet it yields 1.75 litres per second, among the best in the area. The water comes from the shallow-to-mid cracks, not from the extra depth below them.

A 100-metre observation well at Hessarghatta (one of a monitored pair) bored through granite-like rock with quartzite. It met four crack bands between 15 and 68 metres and yields 1.75 litres per second, matching the deeper Hessarghatta well beside it, which suggests the productive cracks here sit in the upper 100 metres.

The shallowest test hole in the study at just over 50 metres, the companion Hessarghatta observation well. Its cracks are all shallow (15-46 m) and it yields only 0.13 litres per second, a thin trickle. Beside its 100-metre neighbour giving 1.75 litres per second, it shows how much yield can vary between two holes in the same ground.

A monitoring well at NIMHANS drilled 100 metres into granite-like rock with light-coloured pegmatite veins. It met two crack bands (roughly 47-51 m and 69-72 m), water stands about 5 metres below ground, and it yields about 1 litre per second: a typical mid-range result for this taluk's fractured rock.

Bangalore North taluk covers 799 square kilometres, about the size of a large city district, and is home to roughly 3.5 lakh people (2011 census) in 199 villages grouped under 39 village councils and 6 hoblies. It gets a modest 870 mm of normal yearly rain. Its corners stretch roughly from longitude 77.37 to 77.74 east and latitude 12.91 to 13.23 north (the report prints the lat/long labels swapped; the numbers are corrected here). It borders Bangalore South, Bangalore East and Bangalore Rural.

This cross-section slices the taluk from north to south through Yelahanka, IISc, Cubbon Park and NIMHANS. Read it like a layer cake: yellow topsoil on top, a pink crumbly weathered layer below it, then a blue lens of cracked water-bearing rock that swells in the middle and pinches out at both ends, sitting on solid red basement rock that rises toward the south. There is no printed depth scale, so thicknesses are approximate, but the message is clear: the water lives in a limited lens of cracks, not in an endless underground lake.

A 3D fence view showing the same four rock layers as the flat cross-section, but in two directions (west-east and south-north) so you can picture how the topsoil, weathered rock, cracked water-bearing lens and solid basement fit together underground. Like the 2D section it has no depth numbers, so treat the thicknesses as sketches of the arrangement, not exact measurements.

The taluk's two-storey water system in one view. Upstairs is Aquifer-I: the shallow water-table aquifer in the crumbly weathered top of the rock, roughly 3 to 33 metres thick. Downstairs is Aquifer-II: water trapped in cracks in the hard granite and gneiss between about 33 and 210 metres down, under pressure. Wells in the study run 50 to 241 metres deep and yield up to 4.26 litres per second. Think of a damp sponge (weathered top) sitting on a cracked concrete slab (fractured rock): most everyday water comes from the sponge, and the cracks below give extra pockets.

The rectangular frame from the report's printed corner coordinates around the whole 799 sq km study area (a locating frame, not a surveyed taluk boundary): Bangalore North taluk with its administrative setting (6 hoblies, 39 councils, 199 villages), corrected corner coordinates, and normal rainfall of 870 mm. Use it as the frame that every other layer sits inside.

Fourteen Central Ground Water Board test and monitoring wells that ground-truth the whole plan. Together they tell one story: yields are mostly small (half the wells give 1 litre per second or less), one deep-cracked well at IISc gives 4.26, and two holes (Rachnehalli and the 310-metre Hessarghatta well) are nearly dry despite their depth. The quilt of depths, crack bands, resting water levels and yields in the table behind these points is the hard evidence that this is thin, patchy, crack-held water. One row (IIM Bannerghatta Road) is table-only because its coordinate looks mistyped.

293 small dams proposed across stream lines to slow monsoon runoff and push it underground. Together the dots show where the plan concentrates its rain-catching effort; the village and council name for each site is listed in the Annexure-I table behind this layer. Every dot is a first-pass pick on a map, not a surveyed building site: the report itself says each spot needs an on-ground check and a detailed project report before construction.

50 recharge ponds proposed to catch and hold rainwater so it seeps underground, listed with village and council names in Annexure-II. Like the check dams, these are tentative map picks needing field verification first, and they cluster in the western two-thirds of the taluk where the ground can actually absorb the water.

About 553 of the taluk's 799 square kilometres, roughly two-thirds and mostly in the west, where the ground is judged suitable for artificial recharge. The built-up city area in the east and south-east is left out because paved ground cannot absorb water. All 343 proposed structures sit inside this zone, and the plan expects it to bank about 5.5 million cubic metres of extra groundwater a year.

Two snapshots of the shallow water table in 2019. Before the monsoon, most of the taluk (65%) sits 5-10 metres down, with a deep 10-20 m pocket in the north-east. After the rains, nearly two-thirds of the area rises to within 2-5 metres of the surface, and only the far north-east corner stays deep. In plain terms the monsoon refills the shallow sponge almost everywhere except the stubborn north-east corner. Zone edges are traced from the report's colour maps, so treat boundaries as approximate.

The landscape setting behind the water story, traced from the report's theme maps. Farmland covers the west and north while the built-up city spreads across the south-east. The ground is mostly flat plain with a low ridge through the middle (peaking at Doddabettahalli, 962 m), cut by branching streams and tanks that drain south into the Cauvery basin. Soils are mostly clayey, formed from the local granite, and one rock unit, banded gneiss, underlies the whole taluk. The paved city fringe in the south-east is exactly where recharge is hardest, linking these maps to the plan.

The underground architecture in section view: a north-south slice plus a 3D fence showing topsoil over weathered rock over a lens of cracked water-bearing rock on solid basement. The lens shape matters, it swells mid-taluk and dies out at the ends, which is why wells succeed in some belts and fail in others. Thicknesses are sketches from figures without depth scales, so read the pattern, not exact metres.

Two pale outlines showing where the evidence actually comes from: one around the 13 mapped test wells, one around the 343 proposed dam and pond sites. They are sample-coverage envelopes, like drawing a loose loop around pins on a map, and must never be read as the taluk boundary or as zones of good water. They answer the honest question of how much ground the dots really cover.

blocks.content: Bangalore North taluk sits just north of Bangalore city: 799 sq km of farmland in the west and north giving way to city sprawl in the south-east, home to about 3.5 lakh people in 199 villages. It gets a modest 870 mm of rain a year. Beneath it lies banded gneiss, a very old granite-like rock, holding water in only two thin arrangements: a shallow weathered sponge (Aquifer-I, roughly 3-33 m thick) and deeper cracks in the hard rock (Aquifer-II, about 33-210 m down). The taluk pumps about 145% of what nature refills, so it is officially classified Over Exploited, and nitrate pollution touches much of the area. The plan answers with 293 small dams, 50 recharge ponds, drip irrigation and strict pumping rules, which together would cut the deficit to about 108%, still over-pumped, but far healthier.
blocks.headline: A thin rocky water reserve under a growing city, pumped half as much again as rain refills

blocks.content: The surface sets up the water problem. Plains cover most of the taluk with a low ridge running through the middle (highest at Doddabettahalli, 962 m), and a branching network of streams and old tanks drains southward into the Cauvery basin. Soils are mostly clayey, formed from the local granite. Land use tells the pressure story: crops in the west and north, dense built-up city across the south-east. Paved city ground cannot absorb rain, which is exactly why the recharge plan skips the urban east and concentrates on the rural west.
blocks.headline: Farmland in the west, city in the south-east, and one rock underneath it all

blocks.content: Think of the underground as a damp sponge sitting on a cracked concrete slab. The sponge is Aquifer-I, the weathered top of the rock (about 3 to 33 m thick), where the water table sits. The slab is Aquifer-II, cracks in hard granite and gneiss between about 33 and 210 m down, holding water under pressure. Fourteen test wells drilled 50 to 310 m prove the pattern: yields are mostly small (half give 1 litre per second or less), one deep-cracked well at IISc gives 4.26, and two holes found almost nothing despite going deep. Depth alone does not make water here; cracks do. The cross-section through Yelahanka, IISc, Cubbon Park and NIMHANS shows the cracked layer as a lens that swells mid-taluk and pinches out at the ends, which is why some belts succeed and others fail.
blocks.headline: A shallow sponge over deep cracks: two aquifers, both thin

blocks.content: The monsoon visibly refills the shallow sponge. Before the 2019 rains, most of the taluk's water table sat 5-10 m down with a deep 10-20 m pocket in the north-east. After the rains, nearly two-thirds of the area rose to within 2-5 m of the surface, and only the far north-east corner stayed deep. The deeper cracked aquifer swings far more wildly, from about 3 m to over 57 m down before the monsoon. The lesson: the rains reliably top up the shallow layer almost everywhere, but the deep north-east stays stubborn.
blocks.headline: The rains refill the shallow layer, except in the stubborn north-east

blocks.content: Only about 2023 hectare-metres can be drawn each year, but pumping runs to about 2932, nearly all of it (2809) for irrigation. That 145% ratio has held since 2009 under every assessment, so this is a long habit, not one bad year. There is no spare water left to promise farmers: the report allows zero future irrigation expansion. Note the 2020 numbers use a revised method, so treat the year-to-year trend as approximate rather than exact.
blocks.headline: Pumping at 145% of refill for over a decade, with nothing left to spare

blocks.content: Most of the water is chemically fine, with one big exception. Saltiness (EC) sits within safe limits in both aquifers, and fluoride is essentially within limits too, with one wrinkle: the printed shallow-aquifer range tops out at 1.56 mg/l, marginally above the 1.5 limit, even though the report text and its fluoride map indicate samples at or below 1.5, so read fluoride as near the limit rather than comfortably clear. Nitrate is the problem: up to 145 mg/l in the shallow aquifer and 129 mg/l in the deep one, against a safe limit of 45, spread across much of the central taluk with safer pockets only at the fringes. Nitrate here comes from human sources such as sewage, fertilisers and waste, so this is pollution, not natural rock chemistry. Any new drinking supply should be tested for nitrate first.
blocks.headline: Safe to drink except for nitrate, which stains the centre of the map

metrics.explanation: Nitrate ranges vs BIS drinking limit
metrics.label: Nitrate vs safe limit

metrics.explanation: Essentially within limits; printed shallow maximum 1.56 marginally exceeds 1.5 while report text/Fig 11 indicate <=1.5 (source inconsistency, Q-07)
metrics.label: Fluoride: within limits

blocks.content: The treatment plan has two halves. On the supply side, about 553 sq km of the rural west can take recharge: 293 small check dams and 50 percolation ponds plus one underground barrier, costing about Rs 39.5 crore, would bank roughly 5.5 million cubic metres a year (a tenth of the runoff they catch). Old tanks (205 of them) get desilted, rooftops and parks drain into filtered wells, and existing borewells can double as recharge points with sand-and-stone filters. On the saving side, drip irrigation on half the fruit and vegetable area (1158 ha) saves about 145 hectare-metres a year. Together the measures lift supply from about 2023 to 2718 and cut pumping pressure from 145% to 108%. Farmers need not change crops, since the report judges these steps enough. But 108% is still over-pumped: this plan shrinks the overdraft, it does not end it.
blocks.headline: Catch more rain, waste less water: the path from 145% to 108%

metrics.explanation: Proposed recharge structures and tentative cost
metrics.label: Recharge package

metrics.explanation: Extra recharge plus drip savings raise usable supply
metrics.label: Recovery math

blocks.content: Three honesty notes travel with this plan. First, every dam and pond dot is a first-pass map pick from the annexure lists; each site needs an on-ground survey and a detailed project report before anyone builds (one well's printed coordinate is already known to be mistyped and is kept off the map). Second, rules must bite: the groundwater authority should reserve water below 100 m for drinking, license industrial use, stop wells being drilled too close together, and require pumping only as needed. Third, the structures only work if maintained, with villagers trained and wells, rainfall and quality measured regularly. Treated city sewage (about 3951 hectare-metres) cannot help here because it is piped away to other districts.
blocks.headline: Map picks are not building sites, and structures only work if maintained
